snapshot.title: UPSC History: The Maratha Empire & Shivaji
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: Ashtapradhan: 8 ministers. Chauth: 1/4. Sardeshmukhi: 10%. Panipat III: 1761. Scindia: Gwalior. Holkar: Indore. Peshwa: Pune.

quick_notes.title: Shivaji Maharaj (1627–1680)
quick_notes.detail: Founded the Maratha Kingdom. Famous for guerrilla warfare (Ganimi Kava). Forts : Raigad (Capital), Pratapgad. Coronation in 1674 at Raigad.
quick_notes.explanation: Shivaji Maharaj lived from 1627 to 1680 and was the founder of the Maratha Kingdom, a powerful state in western India. He is famous for using guerrilla warfare, which is a fighting method that uses surprise attacks, quick movements, and knowledge of the local terrain to defeat larger armies; in the Marathi language this tactic is called Ganimi Kava. Shivaji Maharaj controlled many strategic forts, including Raigad, which served as his capital, and Pratapgad, a key military fort. He was formally crowned as the Chhatrapati (king) of the Maratha Kingdom in a grand ceremony held in 1674 at Raigad fort.

quick_notes.title: Ashtapradhan (Council of 8)
quick_notes.detail: 1. Peshwa (PM). 2. Amatya (Finance). 3. Mantri (Intelligence). 4. Sachiv (Correspondence). 5. Sumant (Foreign). 6. Senapati (Military). 7. Panditrao (Religious). 8. Nyayadhish (Justice).
quick_notes.explanation: Ashtapradhan, meaning council of eight, was the group of eight ministers who helped the Maratha king Shivaji govern his empire. The first minister, Peshwa, acted as the prime minister in charge of overall administration. Amatya managed the kingdom's finances and revenue, while Mantri handled intelligence and spying. Sachiv was responsible for official correspondence and record-keeping, and Sumant dealt with foreign affairs and diplomacy. Senapati led the military forces, Panditrao oversaw religious matters and charity, and Nyayadhish served as the chief justice who decided court cases and upheld law.

quick_notes.title: Maratha Taxation
quick_notes.detail: Chauth: 1/4th of revenue paid by non-Maratha territories to avoid Maratha raids. Sardeshmukhi : Additional 10% tax paid to Shivaji as the hereditary head (Sardeshmukh) of the land.
quick_notes.explanation: The Maratha Empire under Shivaji collected two main taxes from areas they did not directly rule. The first tax was called Chauth, which means one-fourth, and it was a payment of 25% of the land's revenue that a non-Maratha territory had to pay to the Marathas in exchange for not being raided or attacked. The second tax was called Sardeshmukhi, which was an extra 10% tax on the same land's revenue, paid directly to Shivaji because he claimed the hereditary right of being the Sardeshmukh, or the chief headman, of the entire region. So, if a village in a neighboring kingdom owed 100 rupees in total revenue, they would pay 25 rupees as Chauth to avoid Maratha attacks and an additional 10 rupees as Sardeshmukhi to Shivaji for his recognized authority. These taxes were a major source of income for the Maratha state and allowed them to fund their military campaigns without directly governing the taxed territories.

quick_notes.title: The Peshwas (1713–1818)
quick_notes.detail: Power shifted from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa (Brahmin PMs). Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I (Soldier-Statesman), Balaji Baji Rao. Third Battle of Panipat (1761): Marathas (Sadashiv Rao Bhau) defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali.
quick_notes.explanation: The Peshwas (1713–1818) were Brahmin Prime Ministers who gradually took over real power from the Chhatrapati, who was the Maratha king. The first powerful Peshwa was Balaji Vishwanath, followed by his son Baji Rao I, known as a Soldier-Statesman for his military and administrative skills, and then Baji Rao's son Balaji Baji Rao. The Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 was a major war where the Maratha army, led by Sadashiv Rao Bhau, was decisively defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali, an Afghan ruler. This defeat severely weakened the Maratha Empire and ended their expansion northward. The Peshwa rule finally ended in 1818 when the British East India Company defeated the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II.

quick_notes.title: Maratha Confederacy
quick_notes.detail: The empire split into 5 centers: Peshwa (Pune), Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaekwad (Baroda), Bhonsle (Nagpur).
quick_notes.explanation: The Maratha Confederacy was a loose alliance of powerful Maratha chiefs that formed after the decline of the central Maratha Empire in the 18th century. The empire broke apart into five main centers of power, each ruled by a different leader. The Peshwa, who was the prime minister, was based in Pune and was originally the most powerful. The other four chiefs were the Scindia family in Gwalior, the Holkar family in Indore, the Gaekwad family in Baroda (now Vadodara), and the Bhonsle family in Nagpur. Each of these chiefs controlled their own territory and army, and they only came together to fight a common enemy, like the British. This loose structure meant the confederacy lacked unity, which made it easier for the British East India Company to defeat the Marathas in the Anglo-Maratha Wars.

topic_title: UPSC History: The Maratha Empire & Shivaji
lesson_intro: Today we study the rise of the 'Mountain Rats'—the Marathas. Under Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, the Marathas challenged the might of the Mughals and established a decentralized but powerful 'Swarajya'. We focus on Shivaji's 'Ashtapradhan' (council of 8 ministers) and the unique Maratha tax system—Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. For UPSC, understanding the transition from Shivaji's kingdom to the 'Peshwa' confederacy and the importance of Maratha guerrilla warfare is essential.
